study.title: Ezekiel 23 The infidelity of Samaria and Jerusalem and the judgment of God
study.overview: Ezekiel 23 presents, in the form of shocking allegory, the spiritual history of two-sisters: Samaria and Jerusalem, that is, the kingdoms of the north and the south. The chapter recalls that both were unfaithful to the LORD, seeking covenants and idols as if they were lovers, and shows that this idolatry was not left unanswered. The text insists that judgment was not arbitrary: it came because the two cities despised the covenant with God, repeated ancient sins, and profaned what was holy. At the same time, the chapter shows that God himself directs history, using foreign nations as instruments of his sentence.

outline.title: Samaria: the old infidelity and the fall
outline.explanation: The first part introduces the two sisters and identifies Samaria with Oholah. The text describes its ancient contamination in Egypt and its attraction to Assyria, portraying political alliances and idolatry as spiritual adultery. The result is ruin: God gives it to lovers themselves, who expose it, plunder and kill it.

outline.title: Jerusalem repeats and aggravates sin
outline.explanation: Jerusalem, identified as Oolibah, saw the fate of Samaria, but he did not learn. On the contrary, his corruption grows, first with Assyria and then with Babylon. The language of the chapter shows that the desire for power, prestige and pagan customs led to a continuous memory of Egypt and an increasingly degraded spiritual sensuality.

outline.title: Unavoidable judgment: the cup of the sister and the final guilt
outline.explanation: God announces that he will raise against Jerusalem the same peoples that she sought and that they will judge her. The chapter combines images of war, public humiliation, exile and death to show the severity of judgment. The guilt is explicitly linked to idolatry, the profanation of the sanctuary and the shedding of blood. The closure states that in suffering the consequences, the people will know that the Lord is God.

study.context: The notes indicate that the chapter treats the kingdoms of Israel and Judah, with their capitals Samaria and Jerusalem, as two sisters in an extensive allegory. They also point out that alliances with Assyria were part of a political strategy of Israel in previous centuries, but they did not bring security. The text also presupposes the history of falling from the northern kingdom before the judgment on Jerusalem, so that the sentence on the city of the south is presented as more serious because she has seen the example of the sister and yet persisted in the same way.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that idolatry is not just a private religious error; it is unfaithfulness of covenant against God Himself. The language of spiritual adultery emphasizes that sin corrupts desires, memory, politics and worship. Samaria and Jerusalem seek security in human powers, but the same powers become instruments of shame and destruction. There is also a strong issue of increasing responsibility: seeing another person's judgment and still following the same path aggravates guilt. In addition, the text shows that God does not lose control of history: he uses foreign nations to execute judgment, without approving their cruelty. The final purpose is to reveal: judgment exists so that the people may know, for sure, that the LORD is God.

scholarViews.insight: The chapter depicts Samaria and Jerusalem as two immoral women, emphasizing that judgment was inevitable and deserved.
The chapter presents the story of the apostasies of Israel and Judah under the image of bodily adultery, drawing attention to the gravity of spiritual infidelity.
The idolatries of Samaria and Jerusalem are represented by the shameful practices of two harlots, with severe judgments announced about both.

questions: In what ways does the text show that political alliances can become an expression of spiritual infidelity?
Why is Jerusalem judged more severely even though he saw the fate of Samaria?
What current forms of idolatry can seem "safe" at first, but end up producing shame and destruction?
study.practice: Read this chapter as a call to the examination of the heart: where are you seeking security, identity, and approval outside the Lord? It confessed any dependence on modern idols such as power, reputation, control or unfair alliances. Instead of repeating the pattern of Samaria and Jerusalem, practice concrete faithfulness through repentance, exclusive worship, daily obedience and rejection of compromises that contradict the will of God. The chapter also asks to remember: remembering the judgment on sin helps to take holiness seriously and not to play with that which profanes communion with God.
study.uncertainty: The allegorical interpretation of Samaria and Jerusalem as two kingdoms is explicitly supported by the notes, but the detailed identification of some names and peoples in 23:23-24 is not safe in the notes; therefore, it was not used as certainty other than what the commentators claim. Nor should the language of adultery be taken literally; the text uses it as a prophetic metaphor for idolatry and infidelity of the covenant.
